title: Have You Ever Met Someone Who Is Very Funny and Isnt Smart
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article makes the case that genuine humor is a strong proxy for cognitive and emotional intelligence, since being funny requires abstract reasoning, creativity, and social awareness. Because directly asking people whether they're funny rarely yields useful answers, the piece offers a set of unusual, playful prompts leaders can use in interviews or casual settings to surface real wit under low-stakes conditions. It frames humor assessment as a practical, low-cost shortcut for gauging intelligence when more formal signals aren't available.
points: Genuine humor draws on abstract reasoning, creativity, and social awareness, making it a proxy for intelligence.
Directly asking if someone is funny rarely produces a useful or honest answer.
Unusual, playful hypothetical questions can surface real wit better than direct questions.
The technique works best as a supplementary read, not a replacement for other assessment.
quotes: As a shortcut to assessing whether someone has the brainpower to tackle a job or position, it is a treasure.
Humor and wit are strong indicators of cognitive and emotional intelligence. It takes abstract reasoning, creativity, and social awareness to be exceptionally funny.
If you want to use humor as a shortcut to intelligence, the better tack is to give people the opportunity to be funny and see how they do.
You wake up and discover you are invisible, but only to co-workers. What do you do with this superpower?
Give people an opening, and funny people will say something comical or amusing.
